en: Founded **17 April 1913** by **Tómas Tómasson** in two basement bedrooms of a rented Reykjavík house — at first just **1%-alcohol malt extract** — and named after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the warrior-poet who once rhymed his way off an executioner's block (the *Höfuðlausn*, "Head-Ransom") and could drink a whole hall under the table. Aspirational branding.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915) — so Tómas sails to **Copenhagen and Germany (1915–17) to learn brewing anyway**, training up for a product his own country just outlawed. Wine creeps back in **1922**, spirits in **1935**, but **beer stays illegal until 1989**. Beer alone, because it read as **Danish** — and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: So Ölgerðin cheats: brews **Egils Pilsner kept just under the legal 2.25%** — beer that technically wasn't beer. A loophole in a glass. (The orange **Appelsín**, drowned in malt every Christmas, came later — **1955**.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson

en: The irony peaks in **1926**: after a state visit from King **Christian X**, Ölgerðin wins the right to style itself the **"royal brewery"** — a Danish royal blessing, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.

en: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of the only **capital-city rivers on Earth with a wild Atlantic salmon run**. About **2,500** shove upstream past the joggers every summer to spawn — and the city was so smitten it **bought the whole river in 1906**. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)

en: The lights? In **1921** they dammed it for **Elliðaárstöð** — **Reykjavík's** first power station and **Iceland's second** hydro plant, switched on by King **Christian X** in person on **27 June 1921** and still running a century later.

en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sat the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, set up by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. The old ground now lies **partly underwater**. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, then flood it. (More on parliaments shortly.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur

en: The heat, too. Reykjavík's hot water did not start with volcanoes, it started **inside the city** — **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells are still working, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** (Yes, the ground gets a lie-down.)

en: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — son of **Ingólfur Arnarson**, Iceland's first settler — set up the **Kjalarnesþing** over on that headland around **900 CE**, **said to be the country's earliest assembly**, a full generation before the national Alþingi of **930**. Tradition even credits Þorsteinn with **consecrating** that later national parliament — so the founder's son didn't just build the prototype, he blessed the sequel. The þing later shuffled down to **Þingnes by Elliðavatn** (the spit we passed) and kept meeting into the **1200s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: To write proper laws, the chieftains didn't reinvent the wheel — they sent one man, **Úlfljótr**, to **Norway for three years** to study the **Gulating law** and adapt it for home. He came back with **Úlfljótur's Law**, Iceland's **first law code** — but with one radical twist the Norwegians didn't have: a parliament with **no king**. That part was all theirs.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: Nothing was written down — Iceland had no writing worth the name — so **Úlfljótur carried the whole code home inside his head**, arriving back around **921** after **three winters** away. What he recited is **Úlfljótslög**, the oldest law this country has, and it was adopted at the founding of the **Alþingi in 930**. Úlfljótur supplied the text. Þingvellir only supplied the venue.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: **Iceland's first legal draftsman has a lake, a farm and a church carrying his name** — **Úlfljótsvatn**, Úlfljótur's water — and almost nobody stops at any of the three. (The church is the fun one: open a guidebook and it was built in **1914**, open the national heritage register and it was built in **1863**, by **Eyjólfur Þorvarðsson**, *forsmiður frá Bakka*. When two dates disagree, take the one with the carpenter in it.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing

en: The famous line **"með lögum skal land byggja"** — with laws shall the land be built — gets hung round Úlfljótur's neck constantly, and **he almost certainly never said it.** It arrives in Iceland with **Járnsíða**, a Norwegian king's code imposed between **1271 and 1274**, in the fuller form **"með lögum skal land vort byggja en eigi með ólögum eyða"**, and the phrasing traces back to Norway's **Frostaþingslög**. That makes it about **three hundred and fifty years too young** to be his.

en: In **930 CE**, Iceland's chieftains gathered at **Þingvellir** and founded the **Alþingi** — the national assembly. They picked the spot because the **Lögberg** ("Law Rock") cliff wall **carried the spoken law** across the valley.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ The Althing

en: The **Lögsögumaður** (Law-Speaker), elected for a **three-year term**, had to recite **a third of the entire legal code from memory each year** — three years to deliver the lot. Drop one clause and you could change a verdict.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ The Althing

en: And there was **no king** — roughly **36 goðar** (chieftain-priests) ran the whole thing by consensus. One law, one people, zero crowns.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ The Althing

en: It met here every summer until **1798**, sat two more summers in Reykjavík, and was then **abolished outright by royal decree on 6 June 1800.** Re-established on **8 March 1843**, it sat again on **1 July 1845** — in Reykjavík, in a school building. So not a thousand unbroken years. A thousand years with a **43-year hole** that Denmark put there.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / ⚖️ The Althing

en: Which is exactly why, on **17 June 1944**, the modern **Republic of Iceland** was proclaimed here rather than in the capital — on the ground where the nation first assembled, in the rain, in front of tens of thousands. They had chosen that ground carefully in the first place: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.

en: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you're standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here; the valley **is** the gap between them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: The cracks have names — **Almannagjá**, the big one you walk through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it's the seam, still ripping. Filling it is **Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's largest natural lake.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: Clear pools like **Silfra** are meltwater that left **Langjökull** glacier **30–100 years ago**, filtered underground through porous lava — **drinkable from your cupped hand**, with underwater visibility up to **120 m**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: 🎬 **On screen:** Almannagjá gorge is the pass to the **Bloody Gate** in *Game of Thrones* (the gate was digitally added above the Öxarárfoss trail), and the park doubled as an otherworldly realm in ***Thor: The Dark World*** (2013).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: It doesn't creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the old assembly ground.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down here from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m** — the medieval parliament met noticeably higher up than the plain you're standing on.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: **Þingvallavatn** isn't just the largest: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, and its bed sits **below sea level** because of the rifting. Nearly **90%** of its water arrives not down rivers but as **cold spring water at 3–4°C**, **Langjökull** meltwater filtered for years through porous lava — which is exactly why **Silfra** runs so absurdly clear.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years** — a snail-eater, a dwarf, a plankton-feeder and a fish-eater. (Evolution branching in place, with nothing to divide them but appetite.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: Follow the **Öxará** past **Öxarárfoss** and you reach a still green pool called **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**, women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** **drowned here**. Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749**, and a memorial plaque now names them.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: More numbers for the lake: it averages **34 metres** deep, sits at roughly **100.5 metres above sea level**, and the catchment feeding it runs to about **1,300 square kilometres** — of which the lake itself is only about **six per cent.** Everything else is plumbing you cannot see.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: About **nine-tenths of everything entering this lake arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava. Only about **one-tenth** comes in as visible surface water, and the main open river doing that job is the **Öxará** — the one that comes over the wall at Þingvellir. The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces here. (The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: The four charr have names worth knowing: **kuðungableikja**, the snail charr, **dvergbleikja**, the dwarf, **murta**, the small open-water one, and **sílableikja**, the fish-eater. **Two feed on the bottom. Two feed in open water.** Same lake, four completely different jobs — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology

en: **Three of the four are genetically distinct from one another.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out genetically muddled — some individuals read as murta, others as crosses between sílableikja and kuðungableikja. en: She is a great deal older than her CV suggests. The story of the Hekla we would recognise today begins **just over 7,000 years ago** — she was already in business long before anyone was here to take notes. **1104** was her **first eruption after the settlement of Iceland** — and it is still **her own largest explosive eruption in historical time.** (The bigger explosive eruption in Iceland's historical record belongs to a rival: **Öræfajökull in 1362.**) She had been quiet for roughly **three centuries** beforehand, which means nobody then alive had the faintest idea what she was capable of.

en: The ash of 1104 went north, and the farming districts of **Þjórsárdalur** and **Hrunamannahreppur** were **abandoned** because of it. en: The Judas story has a date and a document. **Within ten to twenty years of 1104** an **English poem** was already asserting that **Judas** — the arch-traitor himself — was imprisoned inside Hekla, and European clergy positively welcomed eruption reports, because to their minds an eruption **proved that Hell existed.** The image that fixed it was a woodcut in the history of the Northern Peoples by the Swedish churchman **Olaus Magnus (1490–1557)**, published in **Venice in 1555**, showing Hekla with a set of tunnels running down out of the mountain. **Vesuvius and Etna never acquired the same reputation** — and Vísindavefur offers the driest explanation available. They were **too close to civilisation.** A volcano safely off the edge of Europe made a far more convincing front door.

en: **Haukadalur** means **"Valley of the Hawks"** — known now for steam, but for two centuries this was a **chieftain's seat**: the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth.

en: **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — settled this farm and became the **patriarch of the Haukdælir**. He ran a famous school here in the 11th century, and one of its boarders, from about **age seven**, was **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148) — who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, the reason Iceland has any firm early dates at all. en: The family stayed at the top for two centuries — bishops, lawmen, and finally **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, the oath-breaker of Örlygsstaðir from the last stop: a **Haukdæling**, made **Iceland's first and only earl in 1258**, four years before the republic he helped bury was handed to Norway.

en: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. It's mostly **dormant** now, but its reliable cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn") goes **every 6–10 minutes**, **15–20 m** high (occasionally 40).
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Watch the **dome** bulge just before it fires: a thin layer of cooler water over near-boiling water below, pressure building until it punches through.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The field sits on the **Hreppar block** — water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam, shoots back up.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, most recently **June 2000** — then dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Geysir / ⛲ Geysir

en: **Gullfoss** ("Golden Falls") drops the **Hvítá** down two staircase tiers, **32 m** total, in a narrow canyon — spray throwing rainbows so consistently it looks staged.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: **Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss / 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss

en: Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)

en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its star farm — a working geothermal greenhouse complex where you can eat lunch among the vines.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Inside, roughly **ten thousand tomato plants** grow under LED lights on **geothermal water** piped straight from the ground, pollinated by **imported Dutch bumblebees** — Iceland has no native pollinator strong enough for tomato flowers, so it flew in a workforce.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouse went up in 1924**, over in **Mosfellssveit**, once growers worked out that geothermal water could both **heat the glasshouse and steam-sterilise the soil**. Here at Reykholt the first greenhouse went up at **Reykholtshver in 1932**, and the **first proper horticultural station followed in 1938**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: **Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** took Friðheimar over in **1995**, built the first large house between **1995 and 2001**, and switched to **year-round tomatoes in 2002**. Before that, Icelandic tomatoes simply stopped in winter.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal energy gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **electric grow-lights** through the dark months. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar

en: No new bloodstock has arrived since roughly the year **1000**, so it's essentially a **closed, disease-naïve population** — one of the purest native breeds on Earth. ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🐎 Icelandic Horses

en: Most breeds have three or four gaits; the Icelandic has up to **five**, including the famous **tölt** — a four-beat running walk so smooth you could carry a full beer and not spill it. The extra gaits trace to a **single gene mutation**.

en: **Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** (Skálholtsskóli, 1056), a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: It gave Iceland its **only saint** — **Þorlákur Þórhallsson**, declared holy by the Alþingi in **1198** and formally made **patron saint of Iceland by the Vatican in 1984**; his feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The **Reformation** arrived on **7 November 1550** with the beheading here of **Jón Arason** — the Catholic bishop of *Hólar*, the northern see — and two of his sons. The Lutheran takeover, sealed in blood on this lawn.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: A **~magnitude-7 earthquake** (South Iceland Seismic Zone) in **1784** levelled the cathedral; the Danes used it to abolish the bishopric and shift the see to a fishing village called **Reykjavík** — formally, in **1801**. (The last bishop to live at Skálholt, **Hannes Finnsson**, died here in **1796**; the lights went out slowly.) The current church is a **1963 reconstruction** — where the blues-rock band **Kaleo** later recorded a track live, because Iceland.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: Its first bishop, from **1056**, was **Ísleifur Gissurarson** — whose son ran the school up at **Haukadalur**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The district around it is **Biskupstungur**, **the bishop's tongues** — the wedge of land between the **Hvítá** and the **Tungufljót**. A **tunga** is a tongue of land between two rivers, and the bishop in the name is the one on that hill.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The church came before the bishop. **Gissur hvíti** — Ísleifur's own father — is said to have raised the **first church at Skálholt** after the conversion at the **Alþingi in the year 1000**, and **Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated the first bishop of Iceland in 1056** and took his seat there. Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The school ran from **the later eleventh century until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / ⛪ Skálholt

en: The 1550 beheading has names and a run-up. **Jón Arason** was executed here on **7 November 1550** together with his sons **Ari** and **the Reverend Björn** — and two years earlier, in **1548**, the Skálholt men had thrown up a **fort east of the churchyard** to hold off his attack, the remains of which are still identifiable on the ground. In **1912** an Englishwoman, **Disney Leith**, paid for a **monument** to him at what is taken to be the execution spot.

en: And where did Iceland's electric age actually start? The count tells it better than any adjective could: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flower growing took off across the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.

en: We're on the **Hengill volcanic system**, a rare **plate-boundary triple junction on dry land**. Water goes down, returns at nearly **300°C**, and spins turbines — the white plumes are **steam**, not smoke. Built up in stages 2006–2011 to **303 MW**, it's **Iceland's largest geothermal power station**.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: After the electricity, the leftover hot water pipes off to heat **more than half of the capital region** — nothing wasted.

en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' Mammoth** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: The trick that makes the whole thing work: the geothermal fluid under us is **hot, corrosive and loaded with dissolved minerals**, and it never goes anywhere near your radiator. It is used to **heat clean groundwater through heat exchangers**, and that clean heated water is what travels to the city. **You get the heat without the chemistry.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Hellisheiði's quieter half is the hot water: **200 MW of thermal output**, about **950 litres per second** down the pipe. Over the ridge sits its older sibling **Nesjavellir** — **Reykjavík bought the farm in 1965** and production still did not begin until **1990**, which is **twenty-five years** of drilling, testing and arguing before one useful litre went anywhere. It now runs at **up to 120 MW of electricity** and **up to 300 MW of thermal**, or as Orka náttúrunnar puts it in the only unit a household understands: **1,640 litres of hot water every second.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → BSÍ / 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun

en: Nesjavellir has grown hard. In the late **1990s** the same station was being reported to Alþingi at **60 MW of electricity and 200 MW of heat** — **the electrical output has since doubled and the heat output is up by half**, on the same hillside, with the same rock. en: Under that ice sits **Katla** — a **~10 km-wide caldera**, summit **1,512 m** — one of Iceland's biggest, angriest volcanoes. The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** (~**595 km²**), a **200–700 m** insulating blanket over a furnace. Being subglacial is the whole danger: she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / Katla

en: She's produced **20+ eruptions since 930 CE**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last major one, **1918**, ran **24 days** and dumped so much flood sediment it **pushed the south coast out about 5 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.

en: The rough interval is **every 40–80 years**; the last major was over **100 years ago** — so by any honest reading she's **overdue.** Her system also produced **Eldgjá** around **939 CE**, one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years, and she leaks so much CO₂ while dormant that one study ranked her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**

en: **Hjörleifshöfði** — a **221 m móberg headland** — is named for **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, sworn **blood-brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, Iceland's first settler**. The two **sailed here together around 874**, then split: Ingólfur let the gods choose his home, following his high-seat pillars to Reykjavík; Hjörleifur — who **refused to sacrifice to any god** — parked at the first headland. **His burial mound still crowns the summit.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / Hjörleifshöfði

en: Come spring, says *Landnámabók*: **one ox** — so his **enslaved Irishmen dragged the plough**. They killed the ox and **blamed a bear**. Iceland **has no bears** — the newcomers just didn't know that yet. When the Norsemen scattered to hunt it, the thralls **ambushed them one by one**, Hjörleifur included, then fled with the women and boats to the islands offshore.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / Hjörleifshöfði

en: Ingólfur found the bodies, tracked the killers to those islands, and killed them all. His eulogy: **"A sad end for a good man, slain by slaves — that's what comes of refusing to sacrifice."** Those islands became the **Vestmannaeyjar** — **"Isles of the West Men,"** the Norse name for **Irish Gaels** — **named after the enslaved men who did the deed.**
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / Hjörleifshöfði

en: The ghost came **three centuries later**. **Katla**, a fearsome housekeeper at the nearby monastery of **Þykkvabæjarklaustur**, owned **magic breeches that never tired**. Shepherd **Barði** borrowed them; she **drowned him in the whey vat**. When sinking whey threatened to expose the body, she fled onto **Mýrdalsjökull** and **leapt into the chasm still called Kötlugjá — "Katla's rift"** — the volcano's vent. Soon after, a **glacial flood burst from the ice**. **The volcano is named after her** — and every eruption, they say, is her temper.
ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / Hjörleifshöfði
